title: Babies receive everything
hook: in the East, infants are baptized, chrismated and given communion together

segments.voice: Yesterday, the iconostasis: a wall of faces that turns out to be a window. Your line was the icon screen. Did a room feel fuller than it looked? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-one.

The baby does not approve. She's been lowered into the warm water of the font three times, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and she's letting the whole church know about it. Then, still damp and wrapped in a towel, she's anointed with holy oil: forehead, eyes, nose, mouth, ears, chest, hands, feet. And later, when the people come forward for communion, the priest lifts a small spoon to her mouth, a tiny portion of the consecrated wine. Baptized. Sealed with the Spirit. Fed at the altar. All before she can say a single word. Today is about the Eastern way of welcoming a child.
screen: `THREE TIMES INTO THE WATER.` → `ANOINTED WITH HOLY OIL.` → `A SPOON AT THE ALTAR.`

segments.voice: First, the three. Catholics call baptism, confirmation and the Eucharist the sacraments of initiation: the way someone is brought all the way into the Church. The Catechism says plainly that in the Eastern rites, the initiation of infants begins with baptism, followed immediately by confirmation and the Eucharist. In the East, confirmation is called chrismation, and the priest anoints with the words: the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit. Second, the West spreads them out. In the Latin Church, babies are baptized, and then come years of learning, before first communion and confirmation later on. The Catechism holds the two side by side and ranks neither: the Eastern way shows the unity of the three sacraments, and the Latin way, by keeping confirmation with the bishop, shows the bond with him. Same three gifts. Different timing. Third, the reason the Catechism gives. When it describes the Eastern churches giving communion to the newly baptized, even little children, it recalls the Lord's words, in the Douay-Rheims: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not." Fourth, grace before understanding. A baby understands none of it. Doesn't know the creed, can't say amen, can't even hold her head up. That's the point both East and West make by baptizing infants at all: grace is a gift, not a prize. The East simply carries that logic all the way to the table. The baby in the towel is the picture: everything given, and nothing yet understood.
screen: `BAPTISM, CHRISMATION, COMMUNION.` · `THE WEST SPREADS THEM OUT.` · `SUFFER THE LITTLE CHILDREN.` · `GRACE BEFORE UNDERSTANDING.` · then, large: `ALL THREE AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for newly baptized babies. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a baby you know, or have held, or simply all the babies being carried to a font somewhere this week. Picture one small face. Then the parents, tired, holding on. Then the godparents, who just promised something large. Hold them for a few breaths. If you pray, you can pray the Our Father for them, slowly, the prayer they'll learn one day. If you don't, simply wish them well: a long life, and people who keep their promises. The bell holds the time.
Babies receive everything. In the Eastern churches, infants are baptized, chrismated and given communion in one celebration. Today's word.
Your line: all three at once. Today, name one thing you were given before you understood it, a language, a family, a faith, a name, and say thank you for it. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: In Eastern Catholic and Orthodox churches, an infant is baptized by triple immersion, chrismated with holy myron, and given communion from a spoon, usually in one celebration; Latin Catholics baptize infants and celebrate first communion and confirmation in later years.

fork.setup: you're the priest. the baby has just been baptized and chrismated, and now the people come forward for communion. what do you do?
options: bless the baby, and wait until she's older.
give her a tiny portion from the spoon.
give communion to the parents only.
fork.reveal: in the Eastern churches the newly baptized, even infants, receive communion. the Catechism links it to "suffer the little children to come unto me."

original.note: Greek: an anointing, the oil of the seal of the Spirit.

trapdoor: what you thought: a baby gets baptized, and the rest comes much later.
what it means: in the Eastern churches an infant receives baptism, chrismation and communion together, all three at once.
what a scholar hears: CCC 1233 and 1244 on Eastern infant initiation, and CCC 1292 on what each practice shows: the unity of initiation, or the bond with the bishop.

sources.quoted: Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Mark 10:14 ('Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not; for of such is the kingdom of God'). CCC 1244 cites the line in a different wording; the script quotes the Douay-Rheims.

CCC 1233 paraphrased closely ('the initiation of infants begins with baptism, followed immediately by confirmation and the Eucharist'). CCC 1292 paraphrased for the two emphases; confirm the voice ranks neither.
Byzantine formula of chrismation ('the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit', CCC 1300) given without quotation marks.

Hook details (triple immersion; anointing of forehead, eyes, ears, mouth, chest, hands, feet; communion by spoon) follow common Byzantine practice; the anointed places vary slightly by church. Confirm.
'Grace is a gift, not a prize' summarizes CCC 1250 (infant baptism shows the pure gratuitousness of grace). Confirm.
Latin practice described generally ('years of learning, before first communion and confirmation later on'); order and ages vary by diocese, so no age is given.

Editor pass: added the nose to the chrismation list (Byzantine practice anoints the nostrils; confirm); replaced the 'On an ordinary day' ending, which repeated across the week and told the listener about their own life.
